messages.content: Write the welcome page new engineers see on their first day at a software company. Around 250 words.

# Welcome

You're here. Somebody has already claimed the seat next to you and has opinions about the coffee.

Today is deliberately light. Your laptop should be on your desk; if it isn't, ping #it-help and someone will walk one over. Sometime this morning your onboarding buddy will find you — that's a real person with a name, assigned before you signed, whose job for the next two weeks is to answer the questions you'd feel silly asking in a channel.

Here's what we care about. Ship something small in your first week. Not a feature — a typo fix, a flaky test, a stale line in a README. The point is to walk the whole path from branch to production once while the stakes are nothing, so that the day you touch billing code you already know where the deploy button lives.

Ask early. We measure onboarding by how fast people feel safe interrupting someone, and the record is a day and a half. Beat it.

A few practical things. Standup is 9:45, fifteen minutes, cameras optional. The wiki is roughly 70% accurate and we'd love your help with the other 30% — you're the only person who will ever read it with fresh eyes, and that expires in about a month. Write down every confusing thing this week. Friday, turn the list into a pull request.

Nobody expects output from you for a while. Read code, break your local environment, get it working again. That's the job today.

Glad you're here.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

output:
# Welcome

You made it. The person next to you got here first and already has a position on the coffee situation.

Today is light on purpose. Your laptop should be waiting at your desk; if it isn't, post in #it-help and someone will walk one over. Before lunch your onboarding buddy will come find you. That's an actual human with a name, picked out before you accepted the offer, and for two weeks their job is fielding the questions you'd be embarrassed to put in a channel.

What matters to us: get something into production this week. Not a feature. A typo, a test that keeps flaking, a README line that went stale two years ago. Walk the whole route from branch to deploy once while nothing is riding on it, so the morning you end up inside billing code you already know which button does what.

Ask early. The thing we actually track is how long it takes before someone feels fine interrupting a stranger. The record is a day and a half. Go beat it.

Logistics. Standup at 9:45, fifteen minutes, camera up to you. The wiki is about 70% right and we'd love help with the rest. You're the last person who will read it without knowing the answers already, and that wears off inside a month. Keep a list of everything confusing this week. On Friday, turn the list into a pull request.

Nobody is waiting on output from you yet. Read code. Break your dev environment, then fix it. That's the assignment.

Glad you're here.
